name: The Uniform Resource Locator
statement: The web address that names where a resource lives and how to fetch it, in a structured form.
statementAccent: names where a resource lives and how to fetch it
meaning: A Uniform Resource Locator, or URL, colloquially known as a web address, is a reference to a resource on the Internet that specifies its location on a computer network and a mechanism for retrieving it. A URL is a specific type of Uniform Resource Identifier, or URI; the terms are often used interchangeably, though technically a URL is a URI that not only names a resource but also locates it, implying the means to access it. A URL has several components in a defined syntax, whose general form is a scheme, then a host with optional user information and port, then a path, then an optional query, then an optional fragment. The scheme, or protocol, such as https, http, ftp, or mailto, comes first, followed by a colon and, for many schemes, two slashes. Then comes the host, or authority, a domain name or address such as www.example.com, optionally with a port number. Next is the path to the resource, such as a page's location, followed by an optional query string, introduced by a question mark and carrying parameters such as an identifier and a sort order, and finally an optional fragment, introduced by a hash and pointing to a part within the resource. An example is https://www.example.com:443/path/page?query=1#section. The URL was created and defined by Tim Berners-Lee, the inventor of the World Wide Web, together with the Internet Engineering Task Force's URI working group, and specified in RFC 1738 in 1994. URLs are how resources on the Web are addressed and linked, fundamental to the Web and to hyperlinking.
mechanism: A URL packs, into a single compact string, everything a program needs both to find a resource and to know how to talk to whatever holds it, by following a structured syntax whose parts each answer a specific question. Reading a URL left to right, the first component is the scheme, which names the protocol or method of access, https or http for web pages, ftp for file transfer, mailto for email addresses, and this tells the client which rules to use; the scheme is followed by a colon, and for schemes that address a network location, by two slashes introducing the authority. The authority identifies where the resource lives: at its core is the host, usually a domain name like www.example.com that DNS will resolve to an IP address, optionally preceded by user information and optionally followed by a colon and a port number specifying which service on the host to contact. After the authority comes the path, a slash-separated sequence naming the specific resource within the host, like a file or endpoint. Two optional parts may follow: a query string, beginning with a question mark, which passes parameters to the resource, often as name-and-value pairs joined by ampersands, used for searches, filters, and application state; and a fragment, beginning with a hash, which points to a particular location or section within the retrieved resource, such as an anchor on a page, and is handled by the client rather than sent to the server. Because a URL is a kind of URI, it both identifies and locates: it names the resource and encodes the means to reach it. This precise, uniform structure is what lets any client parse any URL and act on it, and it is the machinery that makes hyperlinks work, each link being a URL that the browser resolves and fetches. Berners-Lee and the URI working group defined this syntax, standardized in RFC 1738 in 1994.

examples.text: In https://www.example.com:443/path/page?query=1#section, the scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment each play a role.
The scheme, like https or ftp or mailto, tells the client how to access the resource.
A query after a question mark passes parameters; a fragment after a hash points within the resource.

whyItMatters: The Uniform Resource Locator is one of the foundational inventions of the World Wide Web, the addressing scheme that makes it possible to name, find, and link any resource on the Internet, and it is so woven into everyday life that its structure is instantly recognizable to billions of people. Tim Berners-Lee's creation of the URL, alongside HTTP and HTML, supplied the missing piece that turned a collection of documents into a navigable web: because every resource has a URL, a uniform address that says both where it is and how to retrieve it, any document can point to any other simply by embedding its URL, and this is exactly what a hyperlink is. That single idea, universal addressing, is what makes the Web a web rather than a set of islands, enabling the linking, sharing, bookmarking, and searching that define online life. The URL's carefully designed syntax, scheme, host, path, query, and fragment, is a small marvel of engineering, general enough to address resources through many different protocols yet simple enough to be typed, spoken, and printed, and its query and fragment components carry the parameters and anchors that power dynamic web applications. Standardized in RFC 1738 in 1994, the URL has proven extraordinarily durable, the stable naming layer beneath decades of web evolution. As the structured web address that names where a resource lives and how to fetch it, the URL is essential to the Web and to hyperlinking.

working.text: begin with the scheme, or protocol, such as https, telling the client how to access the resource.
give the host, and optional port, identifying where the resource lives on the network.
add the path, and optional query and fragment, to pinpoint the resource and a part within it.

limits: The URL is fundamental but several points reward care. The relationship between URL and URI causes confusion: a URL is a specific kind of URI, one that locates as well as identifies, and while the terms are often used interchangeably in practice, they are not strictly synonymous, so conflating them carelessly can mislead. URLs locate resources by where they are, so they are inherently fragile: if a resource moves or a site reorganizes, its URL breaks, producing the familiar dead link, or link rot, which is why persistent identifier schemes exist to address the problem. A URL's syntax has subtleties, including which characters must be percent-encoded and how the fragment, handled by the client, differs from the query, sent to the server, so treating a URL as a plain opaque string can cause errors. Some historical and technical details reward care: the URL was defined by Tim Berners-Lee together with the IETF URI working group, and RFC 1738, published in December 1994 with co-authors including Larry Masinter and Mark McCahill, is the original specification, now superseded by later standards though the 1994 origin is correct; and the general syntax is scheme, authority with host and optional port, path, optional query, and optional fragment. So the URL robustly names and locates web resources, understood as a specific kind of URI whose location-based nature makes links fragile and whose syntax has real subtleties.
misreadings: A URL is not exactly the same as a URI; it is a URI that also locates, not merely identifies. It is not permanent, since resources move and links rot. And it is not an opaque string but a structured syntax with encoding rules and a client-side fragment, so treating URL and URI as identical, as stable forever, or as structureless, misreads it.
origin: The web-addressing scheme defined by Tim Berners-Lee with the IETF URI working group and specified in RFC 1738 in 1994, which names a resource's location and the mechanism to retrieve it.
